clue.text: Novelist means to track man with Chinese porcelain

indicators.note: to track someone is to follow behind them, so the means comes after the other pieces

parts.note: a man is referred to as he
Ming vases come from the Ming dynasty
a means of doing something is a way

explanation.surface: A novelist tracking down a man who owns a Chinese vase.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads the means first, but 'to track' puts it behind the man and the porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Ernest Hemingway, author of The Old Man and the Sea, is one novelist among many.

clue.text: Had me and cast developed using manual skills?

indicators.note: to cast is to pour into a mould and give a new shape, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone boasting that they and a cast of actors grew by working with their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is taken letter for letter, and 'cast' reads like a theatre cast rather than an instruction to remould.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: something made by hand rather than machine has been produced using manual skills.

clue.text: Pot noodle

definitions.meaning: a drinking vessel with a handle
slang for the head or face

explanation.surface: An instant snack in a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: Together the words suggest a Pot Noodle, a British brand of instant noodles in a cup; separately each is a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a mug is a pot for tea, and mug, like noodle, is slang for the face or head, as in 'ugly mug'.

clue.text: Circle filling part of body? Hangman uses this

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, as in a sandwich, so the circle goes inside the body part

parts.note: the nose is part of the body
the letter O is a circle

explanation.surface: A riddle about a ring on the body leading to the gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: The circle sits after the first two letters of the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the looped rope is the hangman's tool, so the whole phrase stands for it.

clue.text: Women's rowing team boosting sport

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for women
a racing crew of eight rowers is an eight
boosting means lifting

explanation.surface: A women's rowing crew giving their sport a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boosting' looks like a verb acting on 'sport', but it is just the last piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: weightlifting is one sport among many, contested at the Olympics.

clue.text: I accept that our time will come after year

indicators.note: coming after means following in sequence, so the year is placed first

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year
taken as it stands
an eon is a long period of time

explanation.surface: A confident prediction that our moment will arrive after a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our' is used as printed, while 'time' means an age.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase is said when taking up a bet or challenge, so it amounts to "I accept".

clue.text: Modest attempt

definitions.meaning: a throw or go at something, as at a fairground stall

explanation.surface: A half-hearted try.
explanation.walkthrough: Together the words read as a small try; apart, each is a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: bashful, and a throw or try, as in a coconut shy at a fair.

clue.text: Dodgy sweet and sour producing wind

indicators.note: dodgy means unsound or unreliable, so the letters cannot be trusted to stay in order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange; 'and' only joins the two words

explanation.surface: A suspect sweet and sour takeaway causing flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is digestive: 'wind' reads as flatulence, but it is the weather sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain sense: a sou'wester is a wind blowing from the south-west.

clue.text: Cry, lacking courage, emitting "ow"

indicators.note: to emit is to send out, so the quoted letters are sent out of the word

parts.note: yellow is slang for cowardly
taken as printed and removed

explanation.surface: A cowardly person crying out in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted 'ow' looks like the cry itself, but it is the part thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cry and a yell are both loud shouts.

clue.text: Cocktail Ronnie mixed with a drop of gin

indicators.note: a cocktail is mixed, so these letters are shaken into a new order
a single drop is the smallest taste, so only the first letter of gin is used

parts.note: the spirit whose first letter supplies the drop

explanation.surface: Ronnie's drink stirred together with a splash of gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a drop of' gives G from gin; 'mixed' rearranges RONNIE plus G.
explanation.definitionFit: A negroni is an Italian cocktail of gin, vermouth and Campari.

clue.text: American university lecturer initially following a routine

indicators.note: the lecturer's letter comes after the a, following it in the answer

parts.note: US is short for American, as in the US

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letter of lecturer is taken

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: An American academic setting out a daily routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives L, which 'following' places after US, U and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Something routine is customary and ordinary, which is what usual describes.

clue.text: Encountered army corps just beyond the yard

parts.note: encountered means met
RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

explanation.surface: Soldiers met just past the back garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The yard looks like a garden, but it is the unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a metre is about 39 inches, a little over the 36-inch yard.

clue.text: Severely criticise Kate changing a role

indicators.note: changing alters the order of the name's letters

parts.note: a part is an actor's role

explanation.surface: An actress named Kate swaps one stage role for another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kate changing' looks like a person altering, but it is the name's letters that change.
explanation.definitionFit: To take apart a person or their work is to criticise them harshly and thoroughly, an idiom.

clue.text: Dog doctor on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a doctor is a healer

explanation.surface: A vet with a radio phone-in show.
explanation.walkthrough: Dog doctor suggests a vet, but 'Dog' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the heeler is a cattle dog breed that herds by nipping at heels.

clue.text: Old relative keeps recording style of garment

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the relative holds the recording

parts.note: a niece is a relative
an extended-play record

explanation.surface: An elderly relative holding on to a recording of how clothes used to be styled.
explanation.walkthrough: An extended-play record, longer than a single but shorter than an album, is a stock crossword recording; it splits the relative after her first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: a one-piece, such as a swimsuit or jumpsuit, is a garment style made as a single piece.

clue.text: Aristocrat somewhere in New Zealand leaving wife for jazz musician

parts.note: a duke is an aristocrat

indicators.note: leaving a place means going out of it, so the wife's letter goes out of the city

parts.note: Wellington is New Zealand's capital
W is the abbreviation for wife, removed

explanation.surface: A nobleman in New Zealand leaving his wife for a jazz player.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a society scandal, but the wife leaving is just one letter dropping out of the city.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Duke Ellington, the bandleader behind Take the A Train, is one jazz musician among many.

clue.text: College pupil from north European country, not south

indicators.note: 'not south' denies the south its place, so the word is written without that letter

parts.note: Estonian means from Estonia
S is the abbreviation for south, removed

explanation.surface: A student arriving from a Baltic country rather than a southern one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From ... country' asks for the adjective of the country, not its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: Eton College is an English private school, and its pupils are known as Etonians.

clue.text: Sack amateur belonging to force

parts.note: lay means non-professional
of expresses belonging
F is the symbol for force in physics

explanation.surface: Dismissing a volunteer from the police force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like the police, but it is the physics symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to lay off staff is to dismiss them, often for lack of work, which is the verb sense of sack.

clue.text: Paddy left son going back

indicators.note: going back means travelling backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Paddy departing after his son heads home.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like a man's name; here it is a British word for a temper tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional synonym: paddy and strop are both British words for a fit of bad temper.

clue.text: Begin small pastry dish

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a tart is a pastry dish

explanation.surface: An instruction to open a meal with a little pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a menu starter; the size abbreviation simply joins the pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to set something going or get under way.

clue.text: Commanding Officer visiting Afghan maybe

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for Commanding Officer
visiting a place is being at it

explanation.surface: A military commander visiting an Afghan person.
explanation.walkthrough: Afghan seems to be a person, but an afghan is also a long sheepskin garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'maybe': an afghan is one kind of sheepskin coat.

clue.text: African animal fine alongside a Greek character

indicators.note: alongside means next to, so the pieces are set side by side

parts.note: fine means OK
taken as printed
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: An African animal doing well beside a Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter here, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the okapi, a forest relative of the giraffe from Congo, is one African animal.

clue.text: Furious with a kid in middle of diner

indicators.note: the a and the kid are placed inside the other letters
the middle of a word is all but its outer letters

parts.note: dropping D and R from diner leaves its middle letters
to kid is to tease, and to rag also means to tease

explanation.surface: An angry customer with a child in the middle of a cafe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child, but here it is the verb to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a rage is an idiom for being extremely angry, the same as furious.

clue.text: Turkish officer appearing in gangway at regular intervals

indicators.note: appearing in means showing up inside, so the letters come from within gangway
evenly spaced, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A Turkish officer standing in the aisle every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: Gangway's even letters give the title; the odd ones are discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical sense: an aga, or agha, was a military commander in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Stuart regularly avoided tasteless stuff

indicators.note: letters avoided at regular spacing are skipped, so every other one is dropped

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Someone called Stuart steering clear of tacky goods.
explanation.walkthrough: Stuart's first, third and fifth letters are the ones avoided.
explanation.definitionFit: A British colloquialism: tat means cheap, tasteless goods or junk.

clue.text: Dark horse's dreadful experience

definitions.meaning: read literally, a female horse of the dark hours

explanation.surface: An unexpected winner's awful ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark horse' is an idiom for an unexpected contender, but here it is read word by word.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: literally a horse of the dark, and figuratively any ordeal as frightening as a bad dream.
